risk_rationale: Inflation remains materially above target on both CPI (3.7%) and PCE (3.6%) measures, with Core PCE at 3.1% keeping the Fed pinned in a restrictive posture. The 10Y at 5.07% with only 27bp of term premium over the 2Y signals a flat curve that continues to compress bank margins and weigh on rate-sensitive sectors. Elevated oil prices ($89.5 WTI / $92.9 Brent), a 3.8% savings rate, and rising credit card delinquencies (2.9%) collectively point to a consumer increasingly under pressure despite resilient headline GDP.
outlook_headline: Resilient growth masks mounting cost-of-capital stress — the lag effects of 5%+ long rates have not fully cleared.
outlook_body: Real GDP growth of 3.4% annualized is running well above trend, but this pace is inconsistent with the Fed's inflation mandate and virtually guarantees no near-term easing cycle. Core PCE at 3.1% and headline PCE at 3.6% leave the Fed with zero room to pivot dovishly, keeping the Fed Funds rate at 3.88% — still accommodative in real terms relative to inflation. The consumer is showing early stress fractures: a 3.8% savings rate, 2.9% credit card delinquencies, and a 7.28% 30-year mortgage rate that has effectively locked the housing market. Any external shock — an oil supply disruption, credit event, or labor market deterioration — would hit a system with limited policy buffer and elevated asset valuations.

tabs.gdp: Q3 2026 real GDP growth of 3.4% annualized is a strong print but increasingly difficult to reconcile with the inflation trajectory — above-trend demand is itself a source of price pressure. Net exports, government spending, or inventory builds may be distorting the headline; the composition matters more than the topline here. The key risk is a sharp deceleration in H1 2027 as 5%+ long rates fully transmit into capex, housing, and consumer credit.
tabs.jobs: 165K NFP MoM is a solid but moderating print, consistent with a labor market that is cooling without cracking. As a lagging indicator, this reading reflects activity from prior months when financial conditions were already tight; forward-looking indicators such as temp employment and job openings will confirm whether the deceleration continues. The trend bears watching — a print below 100K would materially shift recession risk assessments.
tabs.unemp: U-3 at 4.1% remains historically low but the U-6 at 7.9% — a 380bp gap — signals meaningful underemployment and labor market slack beneath the headline. This divergence suggests workers are accepting part-time or sub-optimal roles rather than exiting the labor force, which is a soft form of deterioration that U-3 alone does not capture. If U-6 continues widening while U-3 holds, the labor market is weaker than headline data implies.
tabs.wages: Nominal wage growth of 3.9% YoY is running above the Fed's implicit comfort zone of ~3.5% when targeting 2% inflation over time. Real wage growth is marginally positive versus headline CPI (3.7%), but that gap is thin enough that any renewed inflation uptick would flip real wages negative again. This level of wage growth is not recessionary, but it sustains service-sector inflation and complicates the Fed's last-mile disinflation problem.
tabs.cpi: September 2026 headline CPI at 3.7% YoY and Core CPI at 2.6% represent a divergence driven in part by energy — WTI near $89.5 is feeding goods and transport prices and poses upside risk to October and November readings. No BLS 12-month CPI change is available for October 2026 due to a data collection gap in October 2025; the September figures are the most current valid YoY comparisons. Core CPI at 2.6% is approaching the Fed's 2% target but is not there yet, and energy passthrough could reverse recent progress on the headline.
tabs.pce: PCE headline at 3.6% and Core PCE at 3.1% confirm that the Fed's preferred inflation gauge remains too hot for any policy pivot. The 3.1% core reading in particular is 110bp above target and consistent with an extended on-hold stance. With the savings rate at just 3.8%, consumers are funding spending by drawing down buffers rather than income growth — this is not a sustainable dynamic and raises downside risk to consumption-driven GDP.
tabs.yield: The 10Y at 5.07% and 2Y at 4.80% produce a 27bp positive slope — technically uninverted but historically thin, offering little signal of market confidence in a soft landing. Fed Funds at 3.88% means the Fed is below both the 2Y and 10Y, leaving real rates positive and financial conditions genuinely restrictive. Unless inflation decelerates sharply, the Fed has no credible path to cuts in the near term and the long end remains vulnerable to further supply-driven selloffs.
tabs.credit: IG OAS at 93bp and HY OAS at 347bp reflect credit markets that are complacent relative to the macro risk backdrop — spreads at these levels price in minimal default risk despite tight financial conditions and rising consumer delinquencies. HY at 347bp is particularly insufficient compensation given the refinancing wall many leveraged issuers face into a 5%+ rate environment. Any growth scare or credit event could reprice HY spreads sharply wider from these compressed levels.
tabs.housing: A 30-year mortgage rate of 7.28% has effectively paralyzed transaction volume by locking in existing homeowners with sub-4% legacy mortgages — supply remains structurally constrained as a result. Housing starts at 1,309K are holding up better than expected, but affordability is at multi-decade lows and new construction cannot compensate for the lock-in effect on existing inventory. Residential investment will remain a drag on GDP, and any shock to employment would amplify stress in the mortgage market quickly.
tabs.oil: WTI at $89.5 and Brent at $92.9 represent an elevated energy price environment that is directly feeding headline inflation and compressing consumer discretionary spending power. At these levels, oil is acting as a de facto additional tax on households already running a 3.8% savings rate. Any supply disruption from geopolitical flashpoints could push crude above $95-$100, reigniting headline CPI and forcing the Fed to stay higher for longer than even the current hawkish consensus expects.
tabs.banks: The near-flat yield curve (27bp 10Y-2Y) is a structural headwind to net interest income as banks fund short and lend long — margin expansion from the 2022-2024 hiking cycle is now being competed away on the deposit side. Credit card delinquencies at 2.9% are rising and merit close attention; this is an early-cycle stress indicator that typically leads broader consumer credit deterioration by 2-3 quarters. Banks with heavy consumer credit exposure and limited fee income diversification face the most concentrated risk in this environment.

signal_flags.note: 110bp above the Fed's 2% target — the most policy-relevant inflation gauge leaves no room for rate cuts and keeps real borrowing costs restrictive across all tenors.

Long-end yields at 5%+ are tightening financial conditions beyond the Fed Funds rate itself; continued supply pressure or inflation re-acceleration could push yields toward 5.25-5.50%, intensifying stress on duration, housing, and leveraged credit.
Elevated energy prices feed directly into headline CPI and PCE, threatening to stall the disinflation trend and complicate Fed communication on the path to 2% inflation.
Spreads are historically tight relative to current macro risks — any growth disappointment or credit event could trigger rapid spread widening given the leveraged borrower refinancing wall ahead.

Below the long-run average and declining, indicating consumers are spending beyond income growth; erosion of this buffer will accelerate the consumption slowdown when credit conditions tighten further.
Rising delinquencies are an early leading indicator of broader consumer credit stress — historically precedes deterioration in auto loans and personal credit by one to two quarters.
At this level, housing affordability is at a generational low, existing home sales are structurally impaired, and any employment shock risks a disorderly adjustment in home prices.

October 2025 CPI was never collected by BLS, making a valid October 2026 YoY comparison impossible; the most recent CPI YoY figure is September 2026 at 3.7%. This gap creates a temporary blind spot in inflation trend monitoring.
